stem: You are starting a new project on the Claude Agent SDK. Which pair of package names is current?

options.text: `pip install claude-code-sdk` and `npm install @anthropic-ai/claude-code`
options.why: These are the old Claude Code SDK names. The migration guide replaces both with the Agent SDK packages.

options.text: `pip install claude-agent-sdk` and `npm install @anthropic-ai/claude-agent-sdk`
options.why: These are the current Python and TypeScript Agent SDK packages; Python imports from `claude_agent_sdk`.

options.text: `pip install anthropic` and `npm install @anthropic-ai/sdk`, the official Anthropic client libraries
options.why: Those are the client SDKs for calling the Claude API directly. They do not include Claude Code's agent loop or built-in tools.

options.text: `pip install anthropic-agents` and `npm install @anthropic-ai/agents`
options.why: Neither name is an Anthropic Agent SDK package.

explanation: The Claude Code SDK was renamed to the Claude Agent SDK. The packages are now `claude-agent-sdk` on PyPI (imported as `claude_agent_sdk`) and `@anthropic-ai/claude-agent-sdk` on npm. Seeing `claude_code_sdk` or `@anthropic-ai/claude-code` imports in a codebase is a sign it still needs migrating.
reference: Claude Agent SDK docs: Migrate to Claude Agent SDK

stem: In the Agent SDK, setting `allowedTools: ["Read", "Grep"]` limits Claude to using only `Read` and `Grep`.

options.text: True
options.why: `allowedTools` is an auto-approve list, not a limit. Tools you did not list are still available to Claude.

options.text: False
options.why: Correct. Listed tools run without approval; unlisted tools stay available, and calls to them that need approval go to the permission mode and `canUseTool`.

explanation: `allowedTools` / `allowed_tools` pre-approves tools. To control which tools exist at all, use `tools` (the base set of built-in tools) or put bare tool names in `disallowedTools`, which removes those tool definitions from the request.
reference: Claude Agent SDK docs: Configure permissions

stem: When you move Python code from `claude-code-sdk` to `claude-agent-sdk`, the options class `ClaudeCodeOptions` is renamed. Type the new class name.
explanation: The Agent SDK v0.1.0 breaking changes rename `ClaudeCodeOptions` to `ClaudeAgentOptions`, imported with `from claude_agent_sdk import query, ClaudeAgentOptions`. The fields (such as `model` and `permission_mode`) keep their names.
reference: Claude Agent SDK docs: Migrate to Claude Agent SDK

stem: On a typical Linux or macOS developer machine, what do you need before your first Agent SDK script can run?

options.text: Node.js 18+ or Python 3.10+, plus a separate global install of the Claude Code CLI that the SDK always shells out to
options.why: Both SDKs bundle a native Claude Code binary, so most installs need no separate Claude Code install.

options.text: Node.js 22+ or Python 3.12+, and a claude.ai login that your end users will share
options.why: The versions are wrong, and third-party products may not offer claude.ai login unless Anthropic has approved it.

options.text: Node.js 18+ or Python 3.10+, the SDK package, and an API key in `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY`
options.why: These are the quickstart prerequisites. The SDK reads the key from the process environment.

options.text: Any Node or Python version, plus an `.env` file next to the script that the SDK loads automatically
options.why: There are minimum versions, and the SDK does not load `.env` files; you must load them yourself, for example with `dotenv`.

explanation: The quickstart lists Node.js 18+ or Python 3.10+ and an Anthropic account. Install the package and set `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY` (or use Bedrock, Vertex or Foundry with their environment variables). The packages bundle a native Claude Code binary. Exceptions include a Python source install with no platform wheel, and `npm ci --omit=optional`, which skips the binary.
reference: Claude Agent SDK docs: Quickstart

stem: An interviewer asks how the Claude Agent SDK differs from the Anthropic client SDK (`anthropic` / `@anthropic-ai/sdk`). Which answer is accurate?

options.text: They are the same library; the Agent SDK is just the client SDK with a different import name
options.why: They are different products. The client SDK calls the Claude API; the Agent SDK embeds Claude Code's agent.

options.text: The Agent SDK sends each request to an Anthropic-hosted sandbox that runs the tools, while the client SDK runs tools on your own machine
options.why: That describes Managed Agents. The Agent SDK runs in a process you operate.

options.text: The client SDK ships Bash, Read and Edit tools, while the Agent SDK only offers raw message calls
options.why: This is backwards. The built-in tools belong to the Agent SDK.

options.text: The Agent SDK runs the Claude Code binary with its tools, permissions, sessions and hooks; the client SDK leaves the loop to you
options.why: This matches the docs' comparison table. The client SDK gives direct API access, plus a beta tool runner if you want help with the loop.

explanation: Use the Agent SDK to embed Claude Code's agent loop in your own Python or TypeScript app, in a process you run. Use the client SDK to call the Messages API directly and own the loop. Use Managed Agents when Anthropic should host the harness and sandbox. Use the Claude Code CLI for interactive terminal work.
reference: Claude Agent SDK docs: Agent SDK overview

stem: Match each requirement with the TypeScript `Options` field that handles it.

options.text: `cwd`
options.why: The session's working directory; defaults to `process.cwd()`.

options.text: `maxTurns`
options.why: Caps tool-use round trips.

options.text: `fallbackModel`
options.why: A backup model, or comma-separated list, used when the primary is overloaded or unavailable.

options.text: `disallowedTools`
options.why: Deny rules; a bare tool name removes that tool from Claude's context.

prompts.text: Run the agent against `/srv/checkout` even though the Node process started elsewhere
Stop an open-ended task after 15 rounds of tool calls
Keep serving when the primary model returns overloaded errors
Make sure Claude never sees the `WebFetch` tool

explanation: `cwd` sets the directory that project settings, skills and file tools resolve against. `maxTurns` counts tool-use round trips. `fallbackModel` switches to a backup model and retries the primary at the start of each user turn. A bare name in `disallowedTools` removes that tool definition from the request.
reference: Claude Agent SDK docs: Configure your agent

stem: Order the values of the Agent SDK `effort` option from least reasoning to most reasoning.

options.text: `"medium"`
`"max"`
`"low"`
`"xhigh"`
`"high"`

explanation: `EffortLevel` is `'low' | 'medium' | 'high' | 'xhigh' | 'max'`. Lower effort uses fewer tokens per turn and suits simple lookups. `xhigh` is only available on the models that support it, and not every model supports the effort parameter. If you leave `effort` unset, Claude Code resolves a level itself.
reference: Claude Agent SDK docs: How the agent loop works (Effort level)

stem: If you call `query()` without a `systemPrompt` (`system_prompt` in Python), the Agent SDK uses Claude Code's full system prompt, the same one `claude -p` uses.

options.text: True
options.why: This was the old Claude Code SDK's behaviour (v0.0.x), not the Agent SDK's.

options.text: False
options.why: Correct. With no system prompt option the SDK sends a minimal prompt that covers tool calling. It leaves out the rest of the `claude_code` preset, including its safety instructions.

explanation: The Agent SDK has three starting points: the minimal default, the `claude_code` preset (optionally with `append`), and a custom string. `claude -p` uses the Claude Code prompt by default, so to match CLI behaviour, set `systemPrompt: { type: "preset", preset: "claude_code" }`.
reference: Claude Agent SDK docs: Modifying system prompts

stem: You are building a Python chat UI on the Agent SDK. Users send follow-up questions based on Claude's last answer, and a Stop button must halt a long-running turn. Which API fits best?

options.text: `ClaudeSDKClient`: connect once, call `query()` for each user message, read with `receive_response()`, and call `interrupt()` for Stop
options.why: `ClaudeSDKClient` reuses one session across exchanges and supports interrupts, which the Python `query()` function does not.

options.text: A new `query()` call per message with `continue_conversation=True`, cancelling the surrounding asyncio task whenever the user presses Stop
options.why: `continue_conversation` can chain one-off calls, but `query()` has no interrupt support. Killing the task is not a documented, clean stop.

options.text: `query()` with a string prompt and `max_turns=1`, so every answer finishes quickly and Stop is never needed
options.why: This limits the agent to one tool round trip and still gives you no interrupt or session reuse.

options.text: The `anthropic` client SDK with a hand-written loop, because the Agent SDK cannot hold a conversation
options.why: The Agent SDK can hold multi-turn conversations; `ClaudeSDKClient` exists for exactly this.

explanation: The Python reference compares the two: `query()` starts a new session by default for one-off tasks, with no interrupts and manual continuation. `ClaudeSDKClient` reuses the session, continues automatically, and supports `interrupt()`, `set_model()` and `set_permission_mode()`. Both support hooks, custom tools and streaming input.
reference: Claude Agent SDK docs: Python SDK reference (Choosing between query() and ClaudeSDKClient)

stem: Your team's coding agent should keep all of Claude Code's tool guidance and safety rules, and also always use `pnpm` instead of `npm`. Which TypeScript option does that with the least risk?

options.text: `systemPrompt: "Always use pnpm instead of npm."`
options.why: A string replaces the whole prompt, so the tool guidance and safety instructions are lost.

options.text: `systemPrompt: { type: "preset", preset: "claude_code", append: "Always use pnpm instead of npm." }`
options.why: The preset keeps Claude Code's prompt and `append` adds your rule at the end. Nothing is removed.

options.text: Leave `systemPrompt` unset and repeat the pnpm rule as the first line of every user prompt the app sends
options.why: With no system prompt option you get the minimal default, not the Claude Code preset, and a rule in the first message can be lost when older context is compacted.

options.text: `systemPrompt: { type: "custom", prompt: "Always use pnpm instead of npm.", snapshot: true }`
options.why: The custom form is still a full replacement. `snapshot` only controls whether the prompt is recorded for the session.

explanation: The docs call preset plus `append` the lowest-risk customization: you get the Claude Code prompt with your instructions added after it. A custom string, in either the string or the `{ type: "custom" }` form, sends only what you write. For rules shared with interactive Claude Code sessions, a project CLAUDE.md is another good home.
reference: Claude Agent SDK docs: Modifying system prompts

stem: Which capabilities are NOT available when you pass `query()` a plain string prompt (single message input) instead of an async iterable of messages? (Choose two.)

options.text: Attaching images directly in the message content
options.why: The docs list direct image attachments as unsupported in single message input.

options.text: Interrupting the run in real time with `interrupt()`
options.why: Real-time interruption needs streaming input. `interrupt()` is documented as available only in streaming input mode.

options.text: Running programmatic hooks such as `PreToolUse`
options.why: Hooks work in both modes; the Python comparison table marks hooks as supported for `query()`.

options.text: Calling custom tools from an in-process SDK MCP server
options.why: Custom tools are supported in both modes.

options.text: Capping the run with `maxTurns`
options.why: `maxTurns` is a normal option; the docs' own single-message example sets it.

options.text: Continuing the previous conversation in a later call with `continue: true`
options.why: Single message input can use session state; the docs show a second `query()` with `continue: true`.

explanation: Streaming input is the recommended mode. It gives you a long-lived session with image uploads, queued messages, interrupts and natural multi-turn context. Single message input is simpler and fits one-shot or stateless jobs, but it does not support direct image attachments, dynamic message queueing, real-time interruption or natural multi-turn conversations.
reference: Claude Agent SDK docs: Streaming Input

stem: An agent fixing failing tests works like this: (1) runs `npm test` with Bash, (2) reads two files, (3) edits a file and re-runs the tests, then (4) replies with text only. With `maxTurns: 2`, where does it stop?

options.text: After step 1, because the user prompt and Claude's first reply already count as two turns
options.why: The user prompt is not a turn. `maxTurns` counts tool-use round trips.

options.text: After step 4; `maxTurns` counts user messages, and this run had only one
options.why: `maxTurns` counts tool-use round trips inside the loop, not user messages.

options.text: After step 2, before the edit, with an `error_max_turns` result
options.why: Steps 1 and 2 are the two allowed tool-use turns. The edit would be a third, so the loop stops there.

options.text: After step 3, because only turns that change files count toward the limit
options.why: Every tool-use round trip counts, including read-only ones.

explanation: A turn is one round trip in which Claude's output includes tool calls, the SDK runs them, and the results go back to Claude. The docs' own example says `max_turns=2` stops this run before the edit step. When the cap is hit, the `ResultMessage` subtype is `error_max_turns` and it has no `result` text.
reference: Claude Agent SDK docs: How the agent loop works (Turns and messages)

stem: A run with `maxBudgetUsd: 0.5` stops when its estimated spend reaches the cap. Type the `subtype` value of the `ResultMessage` it ends with.
explanation: When either cap is hit, the result's subtype names it: `error_max_turns` or `error_max_budget_usd`. Neither carries a `result` field, but both still carry `total_cost_usd`, `usage`, `num_turns` and `session_id`, so you can log the spend and resume.
reference: Claude Agent SDK docs: How the agent loop works (Handle the result)

stem: In a monorepo tool, the user switches from `packages/web` to `packages/api` in the middle of an Agent SDK session. The new package has its own `.claude/settings.json` and skills, and these must apply. What should you do?

options.text: Add `packages/api` to `additionalDirectories` on the running session
options.why: Additional directories grant file access, not configuration. Project `settings.json` and hooks load only from `<cwd>/.claude/`.

options.text: Call `applyFlagSettings({ cwd: "packages/api" })` on the query object
options.why: `applyFlagSettings` takes settings-file keys, and the working directory is not one of them. The SDK has no setter for `cwd`.

options.text: Send `cd packages/api` as the next prompt so the Bash tool changes directory
options.why: This changes a shell's directory at most. Claude Code reads project settings, hooks and skills from the session's working directory.

options.text: Start a new session with `cwd` set to `packages/api`
options.why: Neither SDK can change `cwd` mid-session; the docs say to start another session with the new `cwd`.

explanation: `cwd` decides which project's settings and hooks load, where skills are discovered, and which project a stored session belongs to. It is fixed for the session. Project `settings.json` and hooks have no parent-directory fallback, although CLAUDE.md files are also read from parent directories.
reference: Claude Agent SDK docs: Configure your agent (Set the working directory)

stem: A team swapped `claude-code-sdk` for `claude-agent-sdk` and renamed the imports. The tests pass, but the agent now skips Claude Code's usual coding conventions and safety caveats. What is the most likely cause?

options.text: The new SDK ignores CLAUDE.md files unless you pass `settingSources: []`
options.why: This is backwards. Omitting `settingSources` loads user, project and local sources, and `[]` turns them all off.

options.text: The default system prompt is now minimal; add `{ type: "preset", preset: "claude_code" }`
options.why: This is the v0.1.0 breaking change: the default became a minimal prompt, so the old behaviour needs the preset.

options.text: The new package defaults to a smaller model, and `model` must be set again
options.why: The model defaults to Claude Code's default model in both. The visible change in tone and safety comes from the system prompt.

options.text: `ClaudeAgentOptions` no longer has a `permission_mode` field, so the agent silently runs in plan mode instead
options.why: `permission_mode` still exists under the same name; only the class was renamed.

explanation: The migration guide lists the system prompt change as a breaking change: v0.0.x used Claude Code's prompt, and from v0.1.0 a minimal prompt is used unless you ask for the preset or pass your own. The settings-sources default was briefly changed in v0.1.0 and then reverted, so omitting it loads filesystem settings as the CLI does.
reference: Claude Agent SDK docs: Migrate to Claude Agent SDK (Breaking changes)

stem: Put the steps for migrating a Python project from `claude-code-sdk` to the Agent SDK in the order the migration guide gives them.

options.text: Change imports from `claude_code_sdk` to `claude_agent_sdk`
`pip uninstall -y claude-code-sdk`
Review the breaking changes: rename `ClaudeCodeOptions` and set the `claude_code` preset if you relied on the old prompt
`pip install claude-agent-sdk` (and replace the name in `requirements.txt` or `pyproject.toml`)

explanation: The guide's Python steps are: uninstall the old package, install the new one, update imports, then review the breaking changes. Those changes are the `ClaudeCodeOptions` to `ClaudeAgentOptions` rename and the new minimal default system prompt. If pip warns that `claude-code-sdk` is not installed, carry on.
reference: Claude Agent SDK docs: Migrate to Claude Agent SDK

stem: Which statement about the Agent SDK's `effort` and `thinking` options is accurate?

options.text: `effort` is a shorthand for `maxThinkingTokens`, so `effort: "low"` disables extended thinking
options.why: `maxThinkingTokens` is deprecated in favour of `thinking`, and `effort` is a separate control rather than a token budget.

options.text: `"xhigh"` behaves the same on every model, and `effort` can only be set for the whole session, never per subagent
options.why: `xhigh` is only for the models that support it, and `AgentDefinition` has its own `effort` field that overrides the session level.

options.text: They are independent: you can run `effort: "low"` with extended thinking enabled, or `effort: "max"` without it
options.why: The agent loop docs say this directly. `effort` sets reasoning depth per response; `thinking` controls thinking blocks.

options.text: Setting `thinking: { type: "disabled" }` makes the SDK reject any `effort` value at startup
options.why: Nothing in the docs or types says this; the two options are set independently.

explanation: `effort` (`low` to `max`) trades latency and token cost for reasoning depth. `thinking` is `{ type: 'adaptive' }` (the default on models that support it), `{ type: 'enabled', budgetTokens }` or `{ type: 'disabled' }`, and it takes precedence over the deprecated `maxThinkingTokens`. Use low effort for routine lookups and higher effort for debugging and refactors.
reference: Claude Agent SDK docs: How the agent loop works (Effort level); TypeScript SDK reference (ThinkingConfig)

stem: You are shipping a SaaS product built on the Agent SDK. Which ways of authenticating the SDK are supported for this? (Choose two.)

options.text: Set `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY` from the Claude Console in the environment of the process that runs the agent
options.why: This is the quickstart's main method. The SDK reads the key from the process environment.

options.text: Set `CLAUDE_CODE_USE_BEDROCK=1` and configure AWS credentials
options.why: Amazon Bedrock is a supported third-party provider. Vertex and Foundry have their own `CLAUDE_CODE_USE_*` variables.

options.text: Let each customer sign in with their claude.ai account and use their plan's rate limits
options.why: Unless Anthropic has approved it, third-party products built on the Agent SDK may not offer claude.ai login or rate limits.

options.text: Put the key in a `.env` file beside the script; the SDK loads it at startup
options.why: The SDK does not load `.env` files. Load them yourself, for example with `dotenv`, before calling the SDK.

options.text: Pass the key as an `apiKey` field on the `query()` options object
options.why: `Options` has no `apiKey` field. Credentials come from the environment, which you can set through `env`.

explanation: Agent SDK products authenticate with an API key, or through Amazon Bedrock, Claude Platform on AWS, Google Cloud's Agent Platform or Microsoft Foundry using environment variables. The docs state that third-party developers may not offer claude.ai login or rate limits without prior approval.
reference: Claude Agent SDK docs: Quickstart; Agent SDK overview

stem: Match each system prompt configuration with what Claude receives.

options.text: No `systemPrompt` option
options.why: The minimal default: support for tool calls and nothing more.

options.text: `{ type: "preset", preset: "claude_code" }`
options.why: Claude Code's own prompt, with tool guidance and safety rules.

options.text: `{ type: "preset", preset: "claude_code", append: "..." }`
options.why: The preset plus your text at the end; nothing removed.

options.text: `"You are a support bot for Acme..."`
options.why: Only what you wrote; you must add any tool guidance and safety rules yourself.

prompts.text: A thin tool-calling loop where the user prompt carries every instruction
An IDE-style coding tool that should behave exactly like Claude Code
The same coding tool, plus your company's commit-message format
A customer-support agent with its own name, scope and persona

explanation: The deciding factor is how closely your agent resembles Claude Code. Agents with a different surface, identity or permission model, and non-coding agents, are better served by a custom prompt. CLAUDE.md is separate: it is injected into the conversation through `settingSources`, whichever system prompt you choose.
reference: Claude Agent SDK docs: Modifying system prompts

stem:
Your SDK agent ignores the repository's `CLAUDE.md` and the allow and deny rules in `.claude/settings.json`, but it does follow your personal `~/.claude/CLAUDE.md`. The options include:

```ts
{
  systemPrompt: { type: "preset", preset: "claude_code" },
  settingSources: ["user"],
  cwd: repoRoot,
}
```

What is the cause?

options.text: `settingSources` omits `"project"`, so repo CLAUDE.md, rules and settings never load
options.why: An explicit list loads only the sources it names. Project instructions and settings need `"project"`.

options.text: The `claude_code` preset replaces CLAUDE.md; switch to a custom string prompt to load it
options.why: CLAUDE.md loading is controlled by setting sources, not by the preset, and works with any system prompt.

options.text: `cwd` must point at `repoRoot/.claude`, not the repository root
options.why: `cwd` should be the project directory. The SDK reads `<cwd>/CLAUDE.md` and `<cwd>/.claude/settings.json` from it.

options.text: Project settings load only in streaming input mode, and this run used a string prompt
options.why: Setting sources load in both input modes.

explanation: Omitting `settingSources` is equivalent to `["user", "project", "local"]`, which matches the CLI. Once you pass a list, include every source you need: `"project"` for repo CLAUDE.md, rules, settings, hooks and skills, and `"local"` for `CLAUDE.local.md` and `settings.local.json`. `[]` turns all three off.
reference: Claude Agent SDK docs: Use Claude Code features in the SDK

options.text: Call the setters before iterating; they only work before the first message is read
options.why: Timing is not the problem. These control methods need streaming input, which a string prompt does not give you.

options.text: Use `ClaudeSDKClient` in TypeScript; the `Query` object has no control methods
options.why: `ClaudeSDKClient` is the Python class. In TypeScript, the `Query` object returned by `query()` has these methods.

options.text: Pass the prompt as an `AsyncIterable<SDKUserMessage>` so the query runs in streaming input mode
options.why: `setModel()`, `setPermissionMode()`, `interrupt()` and `applyFlagSettings()` are documented as available only in streaming input mode.

options.text: Set `fallbackModel: "claude-opus-5"` and `permissionMode: "acceptEdits"` in the original options
options.why: A fallback model is only used when the primary is overloaded or unavailable, and this removes the mid-session switch the requirement asks for.

explanation: In TypeScript, the control methods live on the `Query` object but need streaming input: a generator that yields `SDKUserMessage` objects (`type: "user"`, `message`, `parent_tool_use_id`). In Python they live on `ClaudeSDKClient`, because `query()` returns a plain iterator. The docs' example holds the second prompt until the setters have run.
reference: Claude Agent SDK docs: Configure your agent (Change configuration mid-session); TypeScript SDK reference (Query object)

stem: A TypeScript job runner calls `query()` with a plain string prompt for each job. An operator needs a Cancel button that ends a running job and cleans up its Claude Code process. Which approach fits this setup?

options.text: Call `q.interrupt()` on the query object when Cancel is pressed
options.why: `interrupt()` is only available in streaming input mode, and these jobs use string prompts.

options.text: Pass an `AbortController` as `abortController` and call `abort()` on Cancel
options.why: The `abortController` option stops the query and cleans up resources in any input mode; `q.close()` also force-ends the subprocess.

options.text: Call `q.setPermissionMode("plan")` so the remaining tool calls are blocked and the job winds down
options.why: Mode changes need streaming input, and plan mode keeps the loop running; it only gates edits.

options.text: Return a deny decision from `canUseTool` for every call after Cancel is pressed
options.why: A denial is fed back to Claude as a tool result, and Claude usually tries another approach, so the loop keeps spending tokens.

explanation: TypeScript has two ways to stop a run: `abortController` ("When aborted, the query will stop and clean up resources") and `Query.close()`, which ends the query, its MCP transports and the CLI subprocess. `interrupt()` stops the current turn of a streaming session that you want to keep alive. Python has no `abortController`; there you use `ClaudeSDKClient.interrupt()` or `disconnect()`.
reference: Claude Agent SDK docs: TypeScript SDK reference (Options, Query object)

stem:
In Python you interrupt a slow task, then ask a new question:

```python
await client.query("Count to 100 slowly using bash sleep")
await asyncio.sleep(2)
await client.interrupt()
await client.query("What is 2 + 2?")
async for m in client.receive_response():
    print(m)
```

The output shows the counting task's messages and a `ResultMessage`, but no answer to 2 + 2. Why?

options.text: `interrupt()` closed the session, so the second `query()` was silently dropped
options.why: `interrupt()` stops the current task; it does not disconnect the client. The second message is still processed.

options.text: `receive_response()` only works once per client; create a new client for each question
options.why: `receive_response()` can be called once per exchange; it stops after each `ResultMessage`.

options.text: The second prompt needs a different `session_id`, otherwise it is merged into the interrupted turn
options.why: Session IDs are not the issue. The leftover messages from the interrupted task are still in the stream.

options.text: `interrupt()` does not clear the buffer, so the first `receive_response()` returns the interrupted task's messages; drain them before reading the new answer
options.why: This is documented buffer behaviour. Read the interrupted task's messages up to its `ResultMessage`, then call `receive_response()` again.

explanation: The Python reference says `interrupt()` sends a stop signal but leaves messages the task already produced, including its `ResultMessage`, in the stream. Drain them with `receive_response()` straight after interrupting. Also avoid `break` out of these async iterations, because it can cause asyncio cleanup problems; use flags instead.
reference: Claude Agent SDK docs: Python SDK reference (ClaudeSDKClient)

stem: A compliance rule says a code-review agent must never even see the definitions of the `Bash`, `Write` or `Edit` tools. Which TypeScript configurations meet that rule on their own? (Choose two.)

options.text: `tools: ["Read", "Grep", "Glob"]`
options.why: `tools` sets the base set of built-in tools, so anything left off the list is not in the request.

options.text: `disallowedTools: ["Bash", "Write", "Edit"]`
options.why: Bare names in deny rules remove those tool definitions from Claude's context before permission checks begin.

options.text: `allowedTools: ["Read", "Grep", "Glob"]`
options.why: This only auto-approves the listed tools. `Bash`, `Write` and `Edit` stay in context.

options.text: `allowedTools: ["Read", "Grep", "Glob"], permissionMode: "dontAsk"`
options.why: Calls to unlisted tools would be denied, but their definitions are still sent; Claude can see and try them.

options.text: `permissionMode: "plan"`
options.why: Plan mode stops edits from being auto-approved, but every tool definition is still present.

options.text: A `canUseTool` callback that denies `Bash`, `Write` and `Edit`
options.why: The callback decides at call time, so the tools are still visible and Claude can try them.

explanation: Three option-level controls do different jobs. `tools` decides which built-in tools exist (`[]` disables them all). `disallowedTools` with a bare name removes a tool, while a scoped rule such as `Bash(rm *)` denies matching calls only. `allowedTools` auto-approves. Permission modes and `canUseTool` decide on calls, not on which tools are visible. The docs pair `allowedTools` with `dontAsk` for a locked-down agent, and point to bare names in `disallowedTools` to remove a tool completely.
reference: Claude Agent SDK docs: Configure permissions (Allow and deny rules)

stem: A CI container runs an agent with `permission_mode="bypassPermissions"` and `allowed_tools=["Read"]`, expecting a read-only agent. The logs show it ran `Bash` and edited files. What is the right fix if the job must keep `bypassPermissions`?

options.text: Also add `"Read"` to `tools`; `allowed_tools` only takes effect when `tools` names the same tools
options.why: `allowed_tools` works on its own; it is simply an auto-approve list, not a limit.

options.text: Add a `can_use_tool` callback that denies everything except `Read`
options.why: In `bypassPermissions` mode, calls are approved before the callback is reached, so this check would be silently skipped.

options.text: Deny `Bash`, `Write` and `Edit` in `disallowed_tools`; `allowed_tools` never limits bypass mode
options.why: Deny rules are checked before the permission mode and block even in `bypassPermissions`. Bare names remove the tools altogether.

options.text: Set `max_turns=1` so the agent cannot get past a single read
options.why: This caps tool round trips; one turn can still contain a `Bash` call or an edit.

explanation: Unlisted tools match no allow rule, so they fall through to the permission mode, where `bypassPermissions` approves them. The permissions guide warns that `allowed_tools=["Read"]` with `bypassPermissions` still approves every tool. Block tools with `disallowed_tools` or a `PreToolUse` hook, or use the `tools` option to remove them.
reference: Claude Agent SDK docs: Configure permissions

stem: You set `maxBudgetUsd: 1.00`. The run ends with `error_max_budget_usd`, but `total_cost_usd` is 1.07 and finance flags it as over budget. What explains the overshoot, and how should you size the cap?

options.text: The cap is a monthly organisation limit, so other sessions pushed the total over; set it in the Console
options.why: `maxBudgetUsd` is a per-query cap enforced by Claude Code, not an organisation or Console limit.

options.text: Subagent spend is not counted against the cap, so subagents add cost on top; disable subagents
options.why: The opposite: subagent spend counts toward the total, and spawning a new subagent fails once the cap is reached.

options.text: The SDK rounds the cap up to the next 10 cents; use a value that is already a multiple of 0.10
options.why: No rounding rule like this exists.

options.text: Spend is checked after each response arrives, so the response that crosses the cap still completes, and running subagents may spend more before stopping; leave headroom
options.why: Cost is known only from the usage each response returns, so the spend can pass the cap by about one response plus subagent spend.

explanation: Claude Code compares the client-side cost estimate with the cap after each model response. The response that crosses it still counts toward `total_cost_usd`, and background subagents still running are stopped. Set the cap below your real limit. In TypeScript, the cap counts only this call's own spend; totals restored from a resumed session do not count.
reference: Claude Agent SDK docs: How the agent loop works (Budget headroom)

stem: A config loader turns an empty field into `0` for both caps. One of them then means "no limit", while for the other the CLI rejects `0` at startup. Type the `maxTurns` value that behaves exactly like leaving `maxTurns` unset.
explanation: `maxTurns: 0` (or `max_turns=0`) runs with no turn limit, the same as leaving it unset. `maxBudgetUsd: 0` is rejected by the CLI as an invalid amount, so the session never runs. A loader that maps "empty" to 0 therefore silently removes the turn cap and breaks the budget cap. Map empty to undefined/`None` instead.
reference: Claude Agent SDK docs: Configure your agent (Limit turns and spend)

stem: A Python batch script loops over 200 repos and runs a single-shot `query()` with `max_turns=20` on each. When repo 37 hits the turn cap, the whole script crashes, even though the code checks `message.subtype == "error_max_turns"`. What is happening?

options.text: Single-shot `query()` raises right after yielding an error result; wrap each repo in try/except
options.why: This is documented: after an error result, the single-shot call raises an error with the failure text, so the subtype branch runs first and the raise follows.

options.text: `error_max_turns` results have no `session_id`, and reading it raises `AttributeError`
options.why: Every result subtype carries `session_id`, `num_turns`, `usage` and `total_cost_usd`.

options.text: The bundled CLI caps a process at 36 queries; create a new event loop every 36 repos
options.why: No such limit exists. The crash comes from the documented raise after an error result.

options.text: `max_turns` is counted across every query in the same process, so later repos start with no turns left
options.why: Each `query()` call has its own cap.

explanation: When a run ends on an error result, a single-shot `query()` yields the final result and then raises (in Python, `ResultError` after an error result), and the Claude Code process exits non-zero. Wrap each run in try/except and keep going. A streaming input session instead stays alive after a cap result, unless the session crashed.
reference: Claude Agent SDK docs: How the agent loop works (Handle the result); Streaming Input

stem: Match each option setting with its effect on Claude's tools.

options.text: `tools: []`
options.why: Turns off every built-in tool.

options.text: `disallowedTools: ["Bash"]`
options.why: Removes the Bash tool definition from the request.

options.text: `disallowedTools: ["Bash(rm *)"]`
options.why: Keeps Bash, but denies matching calls in every mode.

options.text: `allowedTools: ["Read"]`
options.why: Auto-approves Read and restricts nothing.

prompts.text: Claude has only the custom MCP tools you pass in; no built-in file or shell tools exist
Claude cannot see or attempt any shell command
Shell commands stay available, but `rm ...` as written is blocked, even under `bypassPermissions`
File reads run without prompting; every other tool still exists and follows the permission mode

explanation: Deny rules come in two forms. A bare name removes the tool before evaluation; a scoped rule is checked at the deny step and blocks even in `bypassPermissions`, but only for the command as written (`/bin/rm` does not match `rm *`). `tools: []` removes built-in tools but leaves MCP tools you configure. `allowedTools` adds allow rules only.
reference: Claude Agent SDK docs: Configure permissions; TypeScript SDK reference (Options)

stem: Your Docker image runs `npm ci --omit=optional` to stay small. On a supported Linux platform, the first `query()` in the container fails because no Claude Code executable can be found. Which fix addresses the cause?

options.text: Set `executable: "node"` so the SDK runs Claude Code under the Node.js runtime and stops looking for the bundled native binary at all
options.why: `executable` picks the JavaScript runtime. It does not bring back the missing native binary.

options.text: Install without skipping optional dependencies, or install Claude Code natively in the image and set `pathToClaudeCodeExecutable`
options.why: The TypeScript SDK ships its binary through npm optional dependencies, so `--omit=optional` drops it even on supported platforms.

options.text: Pass `settingSources: []` so the SDK stops looking for a user-level Claude Code install
options.why: Setting sources control which settings files load; they have nothing to do with finding the binary.

options.text: Add `@anthropic-ai/claude-code` back as a dependency; the Agent SDK imports it at runtime
options.why: That is the old SDK package name. The Agent SDK does not import it.

explanation: Both SDKs bundle a native Claude Code binary, but some installs end up without one. On TypeScript this happens when optional dependencies are skipped; on Python, when pip installs a source distribution instead of a platform wheel (for example on ARM64 Windows). In those cases, install Claude Code natively and point the SDK at it with `pathToClaudeCodeExecutable` (TypeScript) or `cli_path` (Python). Python also finds it on `PATH`.
reference: Claude Agent SDK docs: Quickstart; TypeScript SDK reference (Options)

stem: For a prompt where Claude runs one Bash command and then answers, put the messages an Agent SDK `query()` yields in the order they arrive.

options.text: A user message carrying the Bash tool result
A result message with the final text, usage, cost and session ID
A system message with subtype `init`
An assistant message containing the Bash `tool_use` block
An assistant message with the text-only answer

explanation: The loop yields an `init` system message with session metadata, then an assistant message for each content block. After each tool runs, a user message carries the tool result back to Claude. The loop ends when Claude replies with no tool calls; the SDK then yields that final assistant message, followed by the `ResultMessage`. A few trailing system events, such as prompt suggestions, can follow the result, so iterate the stream to the end.
reference: Claude Agent SDK docs: How the agent loop works

stem: A reviewer asks what actually happens when your service calls `query()` and Claude decides to run `Bash` with `npm test`. Which description is accurate?

options.text: The SDK sends the tool call to Anthropic, which runs `npm test` in a hosted sandbox and returns the output
options.why: That describes Managed Agents. With the Agent SDK, tools run where your process runs.

options.text: The SDK returns the `tool_use` block to your code, and you must run the command and send back a `tool_result`
options.why: That is the client SDK's manual tool loop. The Agent SDK runs built-in tools itself.

options.text: The SDK runs the bundled Claude Code binary as a subprocess; that process runs the agent loop and executes `npm test` on the host or container where it runs
options.why: The SDK is a library that runs the Claude Code binary, and Claude executes tools directly instead of asking you to implement them.

options.text: The model runs `npm test` inside its own context window and returns the simulated output
options.why: Models do not execute commands. A tool runs as a real process on the agent's host.

explanation: The Agent SDK embeds Claude Code: it starts the Claude Code process, which calls the API, runs tools such as Bash in the host environment, and streams messages back to your code. This is why you need to think about the working directory, permissions and sandboxing. It is also why hosting means running that process (for example, a container per session) and why `spawnClaudeCodeProcess` can move it into a VM.
reference: Claude Agent SDK docs: Agent SDK overview; How the agent loop works

stem: In the Python Agent SDK, `query()` accepts an async iterable of message dicts as streaming input, yet it still does not support interrupts; you need `ClaudeSDKClient` for those.

options.text: True
options.why: Correct. The Python comparison table marks streaming input as supported for both, but interrupts only for `ClaudeSDKClient`.

options.text: False
options.why: The Python `query()` returns a plain async iterator with no control methods, so it cannot interrupt even with streaming input.

explanation: This is where the two languages differ. In TypeScript, `query()` returns a `Query` object whose `interrupt()`, `setModel()` and `setPermissionMode()` work once the prompt is an async iterable. In Python, `query()` returns a plain iterator, so those controls live on `ClaudeSDKClient`.
reference: Claude Agent SDK docs: Python SDK reference; Configure your agent

stem: Your app resumes long-lived sessions with `resume`. When a user switches their workspace to read-only, the app resumes the session with a new `append` line, "The workspace is read-only; do not edit files." Claude keeps proposing edits on the next turn. The settings and the preset are correct. What is going on, and what is the production fix?

options.text: `append` applies only to custom prompts; switch the session to a custom string containing the read-only rule
options.why: `append` belongs to the preset form. A custom prompt would also be recorded and ignored on resume, and you would lose the preset.

options.text: Set `excludeDynamicSections: true` so the new `append` is sent as part of the dynamic user message
options.why: That option moves per-user context out of the system prompt for cache reuse. It does not make a changed `append` take effect.

options.text: The system prompt is recorded on the session's first request and reused until compaction; send the change in the conversation, for example in the next user message or as hook `additionalContext`
options.why: This is documented: a different `append` on resume is not seen. Mid-session instruction changes belong in the conversation, which keeps the recorded prompt and its cache intact.

options.text: Set `snapshot: false` permanently so every request rebuilds the prompt with the latest `append`
options.why: This works, but the docs reserve it for iterating on wording. In production it breaks prompt-cache reuse and can drop earlier thinking.

explanation: By default, Claude Code records the system prompt the first time it renders a session, and sends that record on every later request and after resume or continue, until compaction. To change instructions while a session runs, put them in the conversation: in the next user message, or as `additionalContext` from a `UserPromptSubmit` or `PostToolUse` hook, phrased as a fact. Keep recording on in production, and use `snapshot: false` only while you iterate on prompt wording.
reference: Claude Agent SDK docs: Modifying system prompts (Change the prompt of an existing session)

stem: A fleet of agents across many machines uses the same `claude_code` preset and the same `append` text, yet cost tracking shows almost no cross-session cache hits on the system prompt. What is the most likely cause, and what is the fix?

options.text: Each repo's CLAUDE.md differs and is part of the system prompt; strip CLAUDE.md with `settingSources: []`
options.why: CLAUDE.md is delivered in the conversation, not the system prompt, so it does not affect system-prompt cache reuse.

options.text: The preset embeds a per-user auto-memory path before `append`; set `excludeDynamicSections: true`
options.why: The docs name this exact cause. The option moves per-user context into the first user message, so identical configurations share a cache entry.

options.text: Switch to a custom string prompt with `excludeDynamicSections: true`
options.why: The SDK ignores `excludeDynamicSections` on a custom prompt; it is honoured only on the preset object.

options.text: Set `snapshot: false` so each request re-renders the prompt and refreshes the cache
options.why: Re-rendering on every request makes cache reuse less likely, not more.

explanation: The auto-memory location defaults to an absolute path under `~/.claude/projects/`, named after where the repo sits on disk, so it differs between users, machines and checkouts. `excludeDynamicSections` (`exclude_dynamic_sections` in Python) leaves only the static preset and your `append` in the system prompt. The trade-off is that auto-memory guidance now sits in a user message and carries slightly less weight.
reference: Claude Agent SDK docs: Modifying system prompts (Improve prompt caching across users and machines)

stem: A TypeScript support agent built on the Agent SDK talks to the Claude API directly (no Bedrock or gateway). Its custom `systemPrompt` string combines 20 KB of fixed triage instructions with a few lines of per-ticket context, such as the customer plan and open ticket count. Every ticket misses the cache on the instructions. Which change keeps the instructions cached while the ticket context varies?

options.text: Put the ticket context first and the instructions after it, in one string
options.why: Caching is prefix-based. A changing first part changes the whole prefix, so the instructions still miss.

options.text: Keep one string and add `excludeDynamicSections: true` in a `{ type: "custom" }` object
options.why: `excludeDynamicSections` is ignored for custom prompts; it only applies to the preset form.

options.text: Move the instructions into `append` on the `claude_code` preset and leave the ticket context in the user prompt
options.why: This could cache, but it swaps in Claude Code's coding persona and safety text, which a support agent with its own identity does not want.

options.text: Pass `systemPrompt: [instructions, SYSTEM_PROMPT_DYNAMIC_BOUNDARY, ticketContext]`
options.why: The SDK sends the strings before the marker and those after it as two blocks, each with its own cache breakpoint, so the static block is reused.

explanation: The array form with `SYSTEM_PROMPT_DYNAMIC_BOUNDARY` exists in TypeScript only. The SDK joins each side of the marker and removes the marker itself. If you leave the marker out, everything becomes one block; with several markers, the first one wins. The split happens only on the Claude API directly or on Claude Platform on AWS. On Bedrock, Google Cloud's Agent Platform, Foundry or an LLM gateway, the whole prompt is sent as one block.
reference: Claude Agent SDK docs: Modifying system prompts (Cache the static part of a custom prompt)

stem: A Python agent loads a 60 KB policy document as its system prompt with `system_prompt=open("policy.md").read()`. It works on Linux CI but fails on Windows laptops before any API request is sent. The policy must stay in the system prompt. What is the fix?

options.text: Use `system_prompt={"type": "file", "path": "policy.md"}`
options.why: A string prompt goes on the subprocess command line, which Windows caps at about 32 KB in total. The file form passes a path instead (`--system-prompt-file`).

options.text: Split it into a list of strings with `SYSTEM_PROMPT_DYNAMIC_BOUNDARY` between the halves
options.why: The array form is TypeScript-only, and in any case it controls caching, not command-line size.

options.text: Raise `max_buffer_size` so the SDK can hold the larger prompt
options.why: `max_buffer_size` limits buffering of the CLI's stdout. It has no effect on spawn arguments.

options.text: Send the policy as the first user message
options.why: This avoids the limit but breaks the requirement: the policy would no longer be the system prompt and could be summarised away during compaction.

explanation: The Python SDK passes a string `system_prompt` as one command-line argument. On Linux, a single argument over roughly 128 KB fails with `Argument list too long`; on Windows the whole command line is capped at roughly 32 KB, so the limit hits much sooner. `SystemPromptFile` (`{"type": "file", "path": ...}`) avoids argv entirely.
reference: Claude Agent SDK docs: Python SDK reference (SystemPromptFile)

stem: You host Agent SDK sessions for many tenants on shared infrastructure. One tenant's host-level configuration and per-directory memory must never leak into another tenant's session. Which measures do the docs call for? (Choose three.)

options.text: Run each tenant in its own filesystem, with a per-tenant `cwd`
options.why: Some inputs are read whatever `settingSources` says, so filesystem separation is the base layer.

options.text: Pass `settingSources: []`
options.why: This turns off user, project and local settings, CLAUDE.md files and `.claude/` skills and commands.

options.text: Set `CLAUDE_CODE_DISABLE_AUTO_MEMORY=1` through `env`
options.why: Auto memory under `~/.claude/projects/<project>/memory/` is loaded even when `settingSources` is `[]`.

options.text: Rely on the default `query()` options, since each session already starts with a fresh context
options.why: The docs warn explicitly against relying on defaults for multi-tenant isolation; by default the SDK loads user, project and local settings.

options.text: Treat `settingSources: []` as also turning off managed policy settings and `~/.claude.json`
options.why: Managed policy settings and the global `~/.claude.json` are read regardless; relocate the config with `CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR` if needed.

options.text: Use the same `cwd` for all tenants but give each a different `sessionId`
options.why: A session ID separates transcripts, not configuration or memory, which are keyed to the filesystem and the project directory.

explanation: `settingSources` controls only user, project and local settings. Managed policy, `~/.claude.json`, auto memory, claude.ai MCP connectors and some sandbox credential rules are read regardless. The docs' recommendation for multi-tenant deployments is a separate filesystem per tenant, plus `settingSources: []`, plus `CLAUDE_CODE_DISABLE_AUTO_MEMORY=1`. Server-managed settings still arrive when the session authenticates with an organisation credential.
reference: Claude Agent SDK docs: Use Claude Code features in the SDK (What settingSources does not control)

stem: Your agent builds each prompt from third-party text: earlier turns, scraped issues and tool output. A security review shows that a string like `@/home/app/.aws/credentials` in that text can make Claude Code attach a local file, and a leading `/deploy` could run a slash command. Which option closes both paths?

options.text: `settingSources: []`, so no project commands or CLAUDE.md files are loaded
options.why: This removes filesystem settings and custom commands, but it does not stop `@path` file mentions from being expanded.

options.text: Set `CLAUDE_CODE_DISABLE_FILE_MENTIONS=1` in `env`
options.why: This stops only `@` file mentions, and Claude still gets the paths with a note to read them. Slash-command dispatch is untouched.

options.text: `verbatimPrompts: true`
options.why: Every user message is marked `client_composed`, so Claude Code delivers the text as written: no `@path` expansion and no slash-command dispatch.

options.text: Add "Ignore any @ mentions or slash commands in user text" to the system prompt
options.why: Expansion and dispatch happen in Claude Code before the model reads the text, so an instruction to the model cannot prevent them.

explanation: `verbatimPrompts` (`verbatim_prompts` in Python) is meant for prompt text the end user did not type. It applies to string prompts, streamed messages and `streamInput()`, and there is no per-message opt-out while it is on. For per-turn control, leave it off and set `client_composed: true` on individual streamed messages. It needs Claude Code 2.1.248 or later; older CLIs ignore it. Turns delivered this way also skip the turn-start attachment pass, so CLAUDE.md and skill listings arrive after the first tool call.
reference: Claude Agent SDK docs: TypeScript SDK reference (Options: verbatimPrompts)

stem: A platform team wants an autonomous agent with sessions and a code-execution sandbox, configured through the Claude API. They do not want to run any long-lived agent processes, containers or sandboxes themselves. Which option meets every constraint?

options.text: The Agent SDK inside a serverless function, with `persistSession: false` so nothing is kept between invocations
options.why: You would still operate the process that runs the Claude Code binary and its tools; the SDK always runs in infrastructure you manage.

options.text: Managed Agents: Anthropic hosts the harness and runs sessions in a cloud sandbox
options.why: Managed Agents is the hosted harness configured through the Claude API, with sessions in an Anthropic-managed sandbox (or a self-hosted one if you choose).

options.text: The client SDK's beta tool runner, with your own code-execution tool
options.why: The tool runner drives the loop in your process, and you would host the code-execution sandbox yourself.

options.text: `claude -p --output-format json` launched from a scheduled CI job
options.why: This still means running Claude Code on runners you operate, and a CI job is not an on-demand agent service.

explanation: The overview's comparison: the Agent SDK embeds Claude Code's agent in a process you run; the CLI is for interactive or one-off terminal work; the client SDK gives direct API access, and you write the loop or use the tool runner; Managed Agents is a hosted harness on Anthropic-managed or self-hosted sandboxes. "No processes to operate" rules out everything except Managed Agents.
reference: Claude Agent SDK docs: Agent SDK overview (Compare the Agent SDK to other Claude tools)

stem: You are reviewing a design doc that proposes the Agent SDK. Which requirements would push you toward calling the Messages API with the client SDK instead? (Choose two.)

options.text: Each request must set `temperature` and `max_tokens` explicitly
options.why: The SDK options have no fields for `temperature`, `top_p` or `max_tokens`; the docs say to call the Messages API when you need them.

options.text: The team must own every tool execution inside its existing service, with no Claude Code binary in the deployment
options.why: The Agent SDK always runs the Claude Code binary. Owning the loop without it is the client SDK's model.

options.text: The agent needs built-in file editing, shell and web search tools
options.why: These come built in with the Agent SDK; with the client SDK you would build them yourself.

options.text: Tool calls must pass through hooks and permission modes before they run
options.why: Hooks and permission modes are Agent SDK features.

options.text: Users must be able to resume or fork a previous conversation
options.why: Session resume and fork are built into the Agent SDK.

options.text: The agent's context should be compacted automatically when it nears the limit
options.why: Automatic compaction is part of the Agent SDK's loop.

explanation: Choose by who runs the loop and what you need to control. The Agent SDK gives you Claude Code's tools, permissions, hooks, sessions and compaction, at the cost of running its binary and giving up some raw request parameters. The client SDK gives full control of each Messages API request, but you write the loop and the tools. For cost and depth inside the Agent SDK, the levers are `effort` and the spend caps.
reference: Claude Agent SDK docs: Agent SDK overview; Configure your agent (Choose a model)

stem: Security wants Claude Code, and so every Bash and file tool it runs, to execute inside a throwaway microVM. Your TypeScript API server, which holds the `query()` call, hooks and `canUseTool` logic, must stay where it is. Which SDK feature is designed for this?

options.text: `pathToClaudeCodeExecutable` pointing at a binary path inside the VM's mounted filesystem
options.why: This only picks which local executable to start; the process would still run on the API server.

options.text: `cwd` set to a directory shared with the VM over NFS
options.why: The tools would still run on the API host, only on a shared directory.

options.text: `sandbox: { enabled: true }` on the API server
options.why: The command sandbox restricts commands on the same host. It does not move the Claude Code process into a separate VM.

options.text: A custom `spawnClaudeCodeProcess` that starts Claude Code inside the VM
options.why: This custom spawn hook exists to run Claude Code in VMs, containers or remote environments in place of the default local spawn.

explanation: `spawnClaudeCodeProcess(options: SpawnOptions) => SpawnedProcess` replaces the default local spawn, so the SDK and your callbacks stay in your process while Claude Code and its tools run elsewhere. `pathToClaudeCodeExecutable` (TypeScript) and `cli_path` (Python) only choose a local binary. In Python, a custom `transport` is the closest equivalent, but the CLI-flag options are not applied to it.
reference: Claude Agent SDK docs: TypeScript SDK reference (Options: spawnClaudeCodeProcess)

stem: A Python service sets `env={"ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL": "https://gateway.internal"}` and works. After a port to TypeScript, the agent no longer starts reliably. Which TypeScript setups route traffic through the gateway and keep `PATH` and `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY` working? (Choose two.)

options.text: `env: { ...process.env, ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL: "https://gateway.internal" }`
options.why: In TypeScript, `env` replaces the subprocess environment, so spreading `process.env` keeps the inherited variables.

options.text: Leave `env` unset, and set `process.env.ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL` before calling `query()`
options.why: When `env` is omitted, the subprocess inherits `process.env`, including the variable you just set.

options.text: `env: { ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL: "https://gateway.internal" }`, as in the Python code
options.why: This is the bug. Python merges `env` over the inherited environment, but TypeScript replaces it, so `PATH`, `HOME` and the API key are lost.

options.text: `env: { ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL: "https://gateway.internal", PATH: process.env.PATH }`
options.why: This keeps `PATH` but still drops `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY` and everything else the subprocess inherited.

options.text: `env: { ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL: "https://gateway.internal", ANTHROPIC_API_KEY: process.env.ANTHROPIC_API_KEY }`
options.why: This keeps the key but replaces everything else, so `PATH` and `HOME` are gone from the subprocess environment.

explanation: The `env` option behaves differently across languages. In TypeScript it replaces the subprocess environment, so spread `process.env`. In Python, your values are merged over the inherited environment and override matching keys. In both, leaving `env` unset inherits the parent environment. Many cross-language ports break on exactly this difference.
reference: Claude Agent SDK docs: Configure your agent (Set environment variables)

stem: A TypeScript streaming session starts with `model: "claude-sonnet-5"`. For one hard question it calls `await q.setModel("claude-opus-5")`, and afterwards calls `await q.setModel()` with no argument to "go back". Later turns are not on Sonnet, and each switch shows a cost spike. What explains this?

options.text: With no argument, `setModel()` switches to Claude Code's default model, not the `model` from options; and each model has its own prompt cache, so after a switch the conversation is recomputed uncached
options.why: Both effects are documented. Pass `"claude-sonnet-5"` explicitly to return, and expect a full uncached request after each switch.

options.text: `setModel()` only takes effect after the session is resumed, so the Opus call never happened and the spike is from retries
options.why: `setModel()` applies to later responses in the running streaming session; no resume is needed.

options.text: Calling `setModel()` with no argument restores `fallbackModel`, which defaults to the largest model
options.why: There is no such fallback rule. `fallbackModel` is only used when the primary is overloaded or unavailable.

options.text: Model switches reset `maxBudgetUsd`, so the agent spends freely after each switch
options.why: Budget accounting is unaffected by model switches. The spike comes from cache misses on the new model.

explanation: The configuration docs say `setModel()` / `set_model()` with no model switches to Claude Code's default model, not the one you passed in options. Prompt caches are per model, so the first request after a switch re-reads the whole conversation at the new model's uncached input rate. Switch models sparingly, and keep the original model ID to switch back explicitly.
reference: Claude Agent SDK docs: Configure your agent (Change configuration mid-session)

stem: A streaming input session runs with `maxTurns: 10` and `maxBudgetUsd: 5`. The user queues several messages. Which statements about how the caps behave across those messages are true? (Choose two.)

options.text: If a turn ends at the max-turns limit while a message is queued, that message starts a new turn, and the turn count starts over for it
options.why: This is documented: the queued message is not folded into the capped turn, and the max-turns count restarts.

options.text: Spend keeps adding up across messages; once it reaches $5, later messages in the conversation end with `error_max_budget_usd`
options.why: The budget is cumulative for the conversation, and a `/clear` starts it over.

options.text: The first cap result closes the session and the SDK raises, just as with a single-shot string prompt
options.why: Only single-shot `query()` raises after an error result. A streaming session stays alive unless it crashes.

options.text: A queued message is added to the capped turn's last model call, so it is answered without tools
options.why: Claude Code does not add it to that call; it starts a new turn.

options.text: Subagents spawned during the session have their own budgets and do not count toward the $5
options.why: Subagent spend counts toward the cap, and spawning another subagent fails once the cap is reached.

options.text: The budget resets at the start of each queued message, like the turn count
options.why: Only the turn count restarts per message. The budget accumulates.

explanation: In a streaming session the two caps work differently. `maxTurns` limits each message's run of tool round trips, while `maxBudgetUsd` is a running total for the whole conversation (including subagents) until `/clear`. Single-shot calls end and raise on a cap; a streaming session returns the cap result and keeps accepting messages.
reference: Claude Agent SDK docs: How the agent loop works (Turns and budget); Configure your agent (Limit turns and spend)
